Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively

vignette:
David, a 56-year-old guitarist who had spent three decades commanding stages, now found his world had shrunk to the four walls of his home studio. The trauma had occurred eight months ago, after a show. An influential promoter, a man whose authority in the local music scene was absolute, had invited him for a "private drink" to discuss a tour. The meeting had ended in a violent sexual assault. The promoter's expensive cologne, a cloyingly sweet scent, had filled the small office. In the struggle, David had hit his head against the desk, the coppery taste of blood in his mouth as he was overpowered. This event shattered not just his sense of safety, but the very narrative of his own life.

The memory of that night never arrives as a coherent story. Instead, it surfaces in vicious, sensory fragments. Some moments are appallingly clear: the specific pattern on the office carpet, the glint of a watch on the promoter's wrist. Other parts are a complete blank, a black hole where the worst of the violence resides. He finds himself constantly pushing the memory away before it can fully form, a desperate mental flinching. When these shards of memory do break through-the scent of the cologne, the feeling of being pinned down-they bring with them an overwhelming conviction that he is in imminent danger, as if the assault is happening all over again in the present moment. This terror is so profound that his only response is to retreat. He cancels meetings with agents, avoids old friends from the music scene he used to see after gigs, and has essentially become a recluse, his world contracting to only the places he deems safe.

His pervasive sense of threat has become the lens through which he views the world. A sudden movement from his wife in the kitchen puts him instantly on guard, his body tensing for a blow. This constant hypervigilance makes it impossible for him to relax enough to let the memory of the assault be processed; any feeling of being unsafe causes his mind to slam the door shut on the past. The feeling of being perpetually endangered also primes him to notice potential threats everywhere. The scent of a floral perfume on a passerby, for instance, is no longer just a smell but an alarm bell that signals imminent harm, sending him into a state of high alert. This constant state of threat has fueled a deep, simmering irritability that he fights to control. He feels a hot rage just beneath the surface but has come to believe that expressing it would be catastrophic, so he swallows it down, a decision that leaves his jaw perpetually aching.

This strategy of suppressing his anger and avoiding all reminders of the trauma has only tightened its grip. By refusing to engage with anyone in a position of authority, he has sabotaged his own career, turning down opportunities that would have once been the lifeblood of his work. His avoidance of old social contacts has left him profoundly isolated, which in turn makes any accidental encounter with a former friend feel intensely triggering and dangerous. Furthermore, these efforts to avoid and suppress have kept the traumatic memory itself in a state of suspended horror. Because he never allows himself to fully recall what happened, it remains a collection of terrifying fragments, each one capable of ambushing him without warning, reinforcing the idea that the world is an unsafe place and that he is fundamentally broken. A movie scene depicting violence can send him fleeing the room, heart pounding, as it connects directly back to the unprocessed core of his own experience.

It was an outburst last week that finally brought David to seek help. His wife, reaching quickly for a dropped glass, made a sudden movement that triggered an explosive, aggressive reaction from him. He didn't touch her, but his shout was so full of raw fury that it left them both shaking. The look of fear in her eyes was more than he could bear. He realized that in his desperate attempt to keep himself safe, he had made his own home, the last safe place on earth, feel dangerous for the person he loved most. He came to therapy not with a clear goal, but with a desperate, fragmented plea: to be able to sit in a room with his wife without flinching, and to one day tell a clear story of what happened, even if only to himself.
